the_finding: THE MEASURE-FIRST TABLE SHIPPED: 14 geo rows (10 counties + 4 city-proper), travel-time dist + mode shares + vehicle availability + official mean commute + SAIPE income/poverty merged per row

TEST-1 (the pre-registered falsifier): Memphis commute BURDEN is NOT worse than its comparison set — mean commute 20.9 min = mid-pack (4/10; longer than OKC/SanAnt/Cincinnati, shorter than Detroit/Chicago/Philly/Jacksonville); the naive 'Memphis = brutal commutes' prior DIES HONESTLY

TEST-2 (the lever that DID fire): transit AVAILABILITY, not commute length — Memphis 0.62% transit commute-share = 2nd-lowest of 10 counties (above only OKC 0.49%); the income-peer set (Cincinnati 2.82%, Detroit 2.33%, Jacksonville 3.37%, Philly 19.8%) runs 3.7x-32x Memphis's level

TEST-3 (the Poverty-band anatomy, Memphis city-proper 1-yr): 25,295 below-poverty workers — 17,669 (69.8%) DRIVE ALONE to work; only 780 of 25,295 (3.1%) reach work by transit; of the 1,751 total transit riders, 44.5% are below poverty: WHERE the one bus line reaches, the poor band uses it — the service is absent, not the demand

TEST-4 (the no-car starve): 14,314 no-vehicle households in Memphis city (5.1%) vs transit riders 1,599 total citywide (5-yr county basis): ~93% of no-car households reach work by some non-transit means (walked/borrowed ride/stay-home) — the car-less-and-car-service-starved cell the founder's ladder question aims at

the commute-time x wage-band table: B08136 mode-mean-minutes confirms the shape (transit riders 42-54 min vs car 21-32 min across all captured counties — the transit penalty is universal; Memphis's gap is SERVICE, and route/schedule counts are the near-zero-capital lever exactly as banked)
